message.content:
I don’t have real‑time data, but you can quickly check the current air quality in Los Angeles using a few reliable sources:

| Source | How to use it | What you’ll see |
|--------|---------------|-----------------|
| **AirNow** (EPA) | Go to [airnow.gov](https://www.airnow.gov/), enter “Los Angeles” or your ZIP code. | Current AQI value, pollutant breakdown (PM₂.₅, O₃, NO₂, etc.), and health advisories. |
| **AQICN** (World Air Quality Index) | Visit [aqicn.org](https://aqicn.org/city/los-angeles/). | Live AQI, trend graphs, and forecast. |
| **Local news sites** (e.g., LA Times, KABC) | Search “LA air quality” or look for a dedicated “Air Quality” section. | Often include maps, alerts, and expert commentary. |
| **Mobile apps** (AirVisual, Plume Labs, BreezoMeter) | Download the app, allow location access. | Real‑time AQI, health recommendations, and historical data. |

### Quick steps to check now:
1. Open your browser or app.  
2. Type “Los Angeles air quality” into a search engine.  
3. Click on a reputable source (AirNow or AQICN are usually the most up‑to‑date).  
4. Look for the AQI number and the pollutant that’s driving it.

If you’re planning outdoor activities, remember that an AQI of 0–50 is “Good,” 51–100 is “Moderate,” 101–150 “Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups,” 151–200 “Unhealthy,” 201–300 “Very Unhealthy,” and 301+ “Hazardous.”  

Feel free to let me know if you’d like a quick summary of what each AQI range means for health!
